strategies.title: Explore Rendering Strategies
strategies.description: Next.js offers multiple rendering strategies to optimize your application's performance, SEO, and user experience. From Client-Side Rendering (CSR) for interactive applications to Static Site Generation (SSG) for maximum performance, Server-Side Rendering (SSR) for dynamic content, and modern approaches like React Server Components (RSC), Streaming, and Partial Prerendering (PPR). Each strategy has its own strengths and use cases, allowing you to choose the best approach for your specific needs.

csr.title: Client-Side Rendering (CSR)
csr.description: Pages are rendered on the client-side after JavaScript loads. Ideal for SPAs, Games, and Dashboards where interactivity is key.

step3.title: Dynamic Content Loaded
step3.description: All content is now visible and interactive
step3.clickToLoad: Click "Load Dynamic Content" to see this step

benefits.title: Benefits x Trade-offs
items: Reduced Server Load: Minimal server processing
tradeoffs: Poor initial SEO: Search engines see empty HTML
Slow Time to First Byte (TTFB): Content loads after JavaScript
High client CPU usage: All rendering on client
No content without JavaScript: Breaks if JS is disabled

implementation.title: How to implement?
implementation.description: CSR uses client-side components with React hooks for interactivity.
points: Use 'use client' directive at the top of the file
Components can use React hooks (useState, useEffect, etc.)
Data fetching happens on the client side
Perfect for interactive features and dynamic updates

ssr.title: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
ssr.description: Pages are rendered on the server for each request. Perfect for E-commerce, Profiles, and Real-time data applications where fresh, personalized content is essential.

step1.title: Server Processing
step1.description: 🔄 Server fetching data and rendering HTML...

step2.title: HTML Sent to Client
step2.description: ✅ Complete HTML with data sent to browser

step3.title: Page Ready
step3.description: Page is immediately visible and interactive

benefits.title: Benefits x Trade-offs
items: SEO Optimized: Search engines can crawl content
Fast Initial Load: HTML ready immediately
Social Sharing: Rich previews for social media
tradeoffs: Higher server load: Server processes every request
Increased latency: Server must render before sending
More server resources: Requires more CPU/memory
Slower for high traffic: Each request hits server

implementation.title: How to implement?
implementation.description: SSR uses async Server Components. In App Router, dynamic rendering is the default for pages with dynamic data.
points: Components are async functions (no 'use client' directive)
Cannot use React hooks (useState, useEffect, etc.)
Use async fetch() for data fetching on the server
Data fetching happens on the server for each request

ssg.title: Static Site Generation (SSG)
ssg.description: Pages are pre-built at build time for maximum performance. Best suited for Blogs, Docs, and Marketing sites with content that doesn't change frequently.
ssg.overview: Overview of SSG with dynamic route examples

step1.title: Build Time Generation
step1.pageGenerated: This page was statically generated for ID "{id}" at build time
step1.pageGeneratedId: This page was statically generated for ID "{id}" at build time

step2.title: CDN Storage
step2.description: 📦 Static HTML files cached on CDN

dynamicRoutes.title: 🚀 Try Dynamic SSG Routes
dynamicRoutes.description: These pages are statically generated at build time for different IDs:
dynamicRoutes.tip: 💡 Each page shows different content generated at build time using generateStaticParams()

benefits.title: Benefits x Trade-offs
items: Cost Effective: Minimal server resources needed
tradeoffs: Stale data: Content only updates on rebuild
Long build times: All pages generated at build
No dynamic content: Can't personalize per user
Rebuild required: Changes need new deployment

implementation.title: How to implement?
implementation.description: SSG uses async Server Components pre-rendered at build time. For dynamic routes like [id], use generateStaticParams() to generate all static pages at build.
points: Components are async functions (no 'use client' directive)
Cannot use React hooks (useState, useEffect, etc.)
Use 'cache: "force-cache"' in fetch for static data
Pages are generated at build time, not on request

isr.title: Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)
isr.description: SSG with timed revalidation that regenerates pages in the background. Excellent for Catalogs, News sites, and Product listings that need periodic updates without full rebuilds.

step3.title: Fresh Content Ready
step3.description: Updated content ready for next request

benefits.title: Benefits x Trade-offs
items: Best of Both Worlds: Static performance + dynamic updates
tradeoffs: Brief staleness: Content may be slightly outdated
Revalidation overhead: Background regeneration costs
Complex caching: Need to manage revalidate times
First request delay: May trigger regeneration

implementation.title: How to implement?
implementation.description: ISR uses async Server Components with page-level revalidation. Use generateStaticParams for dynamic routes.
points: Components are async functions (no 'use client' directive)
Cannot use React hooks (useState, useEffect, etc.)
Add 'export const revalidate = 3600' at page level (1 hour)
Use generateStaticParams() for dynamic routes
Use revalidatePath() or revalidateTag() for on-demand revalidation
Set 'dynamic = "force-static"' for static generation with revalidation

rsc.title: React Server Components (RSC)
rsc.description: Server-only components for optimal performance, default in App Router. Ideal for Modern apps, Data-heavy applications, and Secure apps requiring server-side logic.

step1.title: Server Component
step1.description: Rendered on server with direct data access
step1.keyPointText: This data was fetched directly on the server, no client-side API calls needed!

step2.title: Client Component
step2.description: Rendered on client with browser APIs

step3.title: Combined Result
step3.subDescription: Optimal performance with secure data access

benefits.title: Benefits x Trade-offs
items: Secure Data Access: Server-side data fetching
Reduced Bundle Size: Less JavaScript to client
tradeoffs: Interactivity split: Need to choose server vs client
Hydration step: Client components need hydration
Learning curve: Understanding server/client boundaries
Serialization limits: Can't pass functions/classes

implementation.title: How to implement?
implementation.description: RSC uses Server Components by default in App Router. Server Components cannot import Client Components.
points: Server Components are async functions (default, no directive needed)
Cannot use React hooks in Server Components
Add 'use client' directive only when you need interactivity
Server Components can fetch data directly, Client Components use hooks

streaming.title: React Streaming
streaming.description: Progressive loading with Suspense boundaries that streams content as it becomes available. Perfect for Dashboards, Real-time applications, and Progressive apps where users benefit from seeing content incrementally.

step1.title: Fast Content (Immediate)
step1.fastContentSubtext: This content appears instantly while other parts are still loading

step2.title: Slow Content (2s delay)
step2.description: Content that takes time to load, wrapped in Suspense

benefits.title: Benefits x Trade-offs
items: Progressive Loading: Fast content appears immediately
Better UX: Users see content as it becomes available
Parallel Loading: Multiple components load independently
Error Boundaries: Isolated error handling per component
tradeoffs: Incremental UI: Layout may shift as content loads
Fallback UX needed: Must design loading states
Complexity: Managing multiple Suspense boundaries
SEO considerations: Some content loads after initial render

implementation.title: How to implement?
implementation.description: Streaming uses Suspense boundaries with async Server Components. Cannot use hooks in Suspense boundaries.
points: Components are async functions (no 'use client' directive)
Cannot use React hooks (including use hook) in Server Components
Wrap async components with Suspense and provide fallback
Use loading.js for route-level loading states
Content streams to the client as it becomes available
Works seamlessly with RSC and fetch options (revalidate)

ppr.title: Partial Prerendering (PPR)
ppr.description: Hybrid technique combining static shells prerendered at build time with dynamic content streamed via Suspense. Best for Hybrid apps, Optimal performance scenarios, and Modern pages that mix static UI with dynamic data.

step1.title: Static Shell
step1.description: Static content prerendered at build time

step2.title: Dynamic Holes
step2.description: Dynamic content streams into static shell
step2.descriptionText: Dynamic content streams into static shell:

step3.title: Hybrid Result
step3.description: ✅ Static shell + dynamic content = optimal performance
step3.subDescription: Best of both worlds: speed + personalization

benefits.title: Benefits x Trade-offs
items: Instant Static Shell: Fast initial page load
Progressive Enhancement: Dynamic content streams in
Optimal UX: Users see content immediately
Flexible Architecture: Mix static and dynamic content
tradeoffs: Suspense complexity: Requires proper Suspense wrappers
Browser buffering delays: May delay dynamic content
Status codes can't change: Set before streaming starts
Experimental: Still evolving API and best practices

comparison.title: PPR Comparison
comparison.bestForValue: Hybrid apps, Optimal perf, Modern pages

implementation.title: How to implement?
implementation.description: PPR combines static shell with dynamic content streaming. Requires React 19 and RSC. Introduced in Next.js 14.1 (experimental), stable in 15+.
points: Enable PPR via experimental ppr setting in next.config.js
Requires React 19 and React Server Components
Wrap dynamic components in <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
Use 'use cache' directive for cacheable dynamic content
Static parts are prerendered at build time
Dynamic parts stream on request - status codes can't change post-stream

ssg.description: Pre-built at build time. Higher build costs for large sites.

rsc.name: React Server Components
rsc.description: Technique for server-only rendering (default in App Router). No client JS for non-interactive parts. Use Cases: Data fetching, secure logic (e.g., API keys). Pros: Smaller bundles, faster FCP, secure. Cons: No state/events (use Client Components for interactivity); serializable props only. Implementation: Omit 'use client' for server; pass props to client-marked files. Server Components cannot import Client Components.

ppr.name: Partial Prerendering
ppr.description: Hybrid technique (not standalone mode): Prerenders static shell at build time; streams dynamic holes via Suspense at request. Introduced in Next.js 14.1 (experimental), stable in 15+; requires React 19 and RSC. Enable via experimental ppr setting in next.config.js. Use Cases: Pages mixing static UI (nav, headers) with dynamic data (user feeds). Pros: Instant shell delivery + parallel dynamic rendering; SEO-friendly. Cons: Requires Suspense wrappers; status codes cannot change post-stream. Implementation: Wrap dynamic components in Suspense with fallback; use cache directive.
